chunks: "Metastability is what happens when a flip-flop's data input changes right at the clock edge, inside its setup and hold window.
A flip-flop is a bistable circuit, basically two cross-coupled inverters, with two stable states, 0 and 1, and an unstable balance point in between, like a ball on the top of a hill.
Normally the input pushes it clearly to one side. If the data changes right at the sampling moment, the internal node can be left near that balance point.
Positive feedback then amplifies whatever tiny difference exists, exponentially, until it falls to 0 or 1, but how long that takes is random and, in principle, unbounded.
During that time the output can sit at an in-between voltage, or oscillate, or switch late.
The danger is that downstream logic sees a value near its threshold, so different gates interpret it differently, giving inconsistent state, and the system can crash.
You can't eliminate it for truly asynchronous signals, so you make failures extremely rare.
The standard fix is a synchronizer: two or more flip-flops in series clocked by the destination clock.
The first one may go metastable, but it has a full clock period to resolve before the second samples it.
The probability of still being unresolved falls exponentially with the time you give it, so the mean time between failures becomes thousands or millions of years.
For multi-bit data you don't synchronize each bit separately; you use a handshake, a Gray-coded counter or an asynchronous FIFO."
